items.title: Top-100 coin basket from the FTX low: $10k became $19.4k. Just BTC: $76.6k
items.idea: Buying $100 of each top-100 coin on 20 Nov 2022 and holding to the 6 Oct 2025 peak gave ~$19,400. The same $10k in BTC gave ~$76,600. Three quarters of the basket's gains came from 10 coins, and the median coin returned 99 cents per dollar, so over half the basket was down at the cycle top. Since the Oct 2025 top the basket is worth ~$5,700 (6 of 100 up) vs ~$6,700 in BTC.
items.angle: Direct evidence that index-the-alts is a negative-alpha trade. Supports barbell: BTC plus a handful of cash-flowing tokens.
items.tweetA: Bought the top 100 coins at the FTX bottom and held through ETFs, the election and the top: 1.9x. Bitcoin alone: 7.7x. The median coin was below cost at the peak. 'Diversification' in crypto was the most expensive hedge of the cycle.
items.tweetB: Ten coins made 75% of the top-100 gains. If you can't name the ten in advance, owning the other 90 isn't diversification, it's a fee on your PnL. $BTC $ETH

charts.desc: Chart: $10k basket of top-100 vs BTC from Nov 2022; per-cycle (2018/2021/2025) one-year-after-top returns for best 5 vs median coin.

items.title: Buybacks went from $190M to $1.85B in five years, and rose through a -33% market
items.idea: Token buybacks/burns: ~$190M in the year to Oct 2021 vs ~$1.85B in the year to Oct 2026; projects spending $1M+ a year went from 10 to 70+. Total crypto market cap fell more than a third over the last year while buyback spend still rose. ~6 in 10 buyback tokens beat BTC over the year vs ~1 in 4 for everything else (BTC itself down ~25%).
items.angle: Crypto's first countercyclical bid. Treat buyback cash as the new 'earnings' line when screening alts.
items.tweetA: Market cap -33% in a year. Buyback spend still went UP. That's the first time crypto has had a bid that doesn't depend on the next buyer showing up. $HYPE $PUMP
items.tweetB: The buyback tokens beat BTC 6 times in 10. Everything else: 1 in 4. Whatever you think of the narrative, the market is already paying for cash flow. Are you still screening alts on TVL and followers?

charts.desc: Bar chart of annual token buyback spend 2021-2026 with the last bar up while market cap fell.

items.title: The crypto P/E: market cap / annual buybacks. Best-run tokens trade ~30x
items.idea: Zeneca's crude multiple: HYPE, JUP, PENDLE and SKY all trade ~30x annual buyback spend. At lows the multiples were absurd: PUMP ~3x (then ~5x), AERO <3x fees to lockers (then >3x), HYPE ~11x in Jan 2026 vs ~27x now. DRV trades >100x revenue and needs 4-6x fee growth to reach 30x. Caveats: where the bought tokens go (burn vs cashback), and unlocks (PUMP unlocks ~$40M/month to insiders until mid-2029).
items.angle: A usable screening heuristic, and a warning: HYPE has re-rated from 11x to 27x, so the easy part is done.
items.tweetA: HYPE bottomed at ~11x annual buybacks in January. It's ~27x now and the token roughly quadrupled. The multiple expanded 2.5x, so most of that move was re-rating. What does the next leg need?
items.tweetB: A $40M/month insider unlock against a buyback is not a buyback, it's a transfer. Check the net, not the headline. $PUMP

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening (buyback multiples at lows vs now).

items.title: ZEC went $50 to $1,300 and most people bought the beta instead
items.idea: ZEC was ~$50 a year ago, now ~$1,300: a 26x. The author's claim is that FOMO traders skip the leader and buy its 'beta' (NEAR, STRK), which is why they lost money in an 'easy mode' tape since 19 Aug. Old coins are bid because they are mostly fully unlocked and solve one thing, and quantum fear (Justin Drake's 'bunker mode', Starknet pitching quantum resistance) is the catalyst. BlockchainCenter alt-season index needs 75% of top-50 beating BTC over 90 days.
items.angle: Pairs with Zeneca: both say narrow leadership. The quantum-risk bid is a new factor to watch in alt dispersion.
items.tweetA: ZEC 26x. Everyone who missed it bought the 'next ZEC' instead. That's the entire alt cycle in one trade: the leader is never cheap enough, so you buy its shadow. $ZEC
items.tweetB: The alt bid in October 2026 is a quantum-risk hedge, not alt season. When 'cryptography might break in months' is the thesis, you're not buying growth, you're buying insurance. $STRK $ZEC

items.title: Ledger users report $86M+ drained; Ledger points to reseller CryptoBillis
items.idea: Specter traced >$86M in theft addresses taking funds from hundreds of wallets across Ethereum, TRON and Bitcoin. Ledger says it is investigating losses among Southeast Asian buyers from reseller CryptoBillis, asked it to halt sales, and told anyone who bought in the last 90 days not to set up the device or to move assets to a new seed. Ledger has not confirmed the $86M figure.
items.angle: Supply-chain attack on the self-custody layer. Reinforces custody, qualified-custodian and ETF demand.
items.tweetA: $86M drained from hardware-wallet users, and the common factor is where the device was bought. The weakest link in self-custody isn't the cryptography, it's the logistics chain. Expect the institutional custody pitch to get louder.
items.tweetB: If a pre-tampered device can drain hundreds of wallets before the vendor notices, 'not your keys, not your coins' needs an addendum: 'not your supply chain'. $BTC $ETH

items.title: CFTC proposes event contracts as swaps; 40 states say it's sports betting
items.idea: CFTC proposed adding event contracts (sports, politics, culture, weather) to its swap definition; Chair Selig calls them 'exclusive jurisdiction'. A companion interim rule keeps sportsbook bets and casino games outside. The courts are split: Third Circuit sided with Kalshi in April, Ninth and Sixth Circuits against, and New Jersey asked SCOTUS to take it in September. Comments due 30 days after Federal Register publication. Blockchain.com has also applied for CFTC licences for prediction markets and derivatives.
items.angle: Federal preemption of states for prediction markets is heading to SCOTUS. Binary outcome for Kalshi/Polymarket/Robinhood volume.
items.tweetA: The CFTC wants prediction markets classified as swaps. 40 states say it's gambling. Three circuits split 1-2. This ends at SCOTUS, and the ruling reprices every venue's US volume.
items.tweetB: A rule defining sports contracts as swaps while carving sportsbooks out of the same definition. That's a line drawn by who has the lobbyists, not by the product. $HOOD

items.title: Kalshi: $173 of bets on a 1% press-secretary pick, 20 minutes before the news
items.idea: Three sub-$100 Kalshi bets ($19, $74, $80) backed Katie Zacharia for White House press secretary before her pick was reported; two landed ~1:41pm ET Friday, <20 minutes before outlets reported it. At ~1% odds the $173 stake would pay ~$9,600. Kalshi is reviewing. Precedent: a former White House teleprompter operator repaid $107,539 in August to settle CFTC charges.
items.angle: Insider-trading enforcement in event markets is the regulatory risk underneath the CFTC jurisdiction fight.
items.tweetA: $173 on a 1% outcome, placed minutes before the leak, for a $9,600 payout. Tiny dollars, but the pattern is the point: prediction markets are the first venue where a staffer's group chat is a tradeable asset.
items.tweetB: Everyone is arguing about whether the CFTC or the states regulate Kalshi. Nobody is asking who surveils 80-dollar bets 20 minutes before a leak. The real supervision gap is this one.

items.title: XRPL fixed a 2015-era overflow that could mint XRP beyond supply, skipping the vote
items.idea: Integer overflow in the payment engine could let an attacker mint spendable XRP far beyond total supply in one transaction; likely present since 2015. Reported via bug bounty on 22 Sept, fixed in xrpld 3.4.1 on 25 Sept, no evidence of exploitation. The fix skipped the >80%-for-two-weeks amendment vote, the first such bypass since amendments began, to avoid advertising the bug. Foundation says ~99.986B XRP exist.
items.angle: Governance precedent: emergency unilateral patch on a 'decentralised' ledger. Also AI-assisted bug discovery (Veria AI).
items.tweetA: XRPL had a bug that could print XRP past the cap for ~11 years. It was found by an AI-assisted researcher and patched without a validator vote. Both halves of that sentence matter more than the bug. $XRP
items.tweetB: A fixed supply is only as fixed as the last unaudited integer. If AI auditors are finding decade-old overflows in a payments ledger, which other 'immutable' codebase is next?

items.title: IMF: most tokenized-stock trading is off-hours, 80% of trades under one share
items.idea: IMF found more than half of tokenized US stock trading happens outside regular market hours, ~80% of trades are for less than one share, and tokens are ~1.5x as volatile as the underlying shares. It called for circuit breakers on tokenized venues.
items.angle: Tokenized equities are a retail, overnight, fractional product, effectively a 24h price-discovery venue for US stocks.
items.tweetA: More than half of tokenized stock volume trades when the NYSE is closed, 80% of trades are sub-share, and the tokens are 1.5x as volatile as the shares. This is a 24-hour retail gap-risk market. Watch Sunday-night tokenized prints against Monday opens.
items.tweetB: The IMF wants circuit breakers on tokenized stocks. The interesting part is the implication: the token market is already where overnight price discovery happens, and the exchange is the lagging venue.

items.title: UK sanctions three crypto exchanges tied to A7, the network behind the ruble stablecoin A7A5
items.idea: UK designated three crypto exchanges and two payment platforms suspected of helping Russia evade sanctions (part of 38 designations). Two allegedly processed transactions with A7, the Kremlin-backed network behind ruble-pegged stablecoin A7A5.
items.angle: Stablecoins as sanctions-evasion rails; also the template for the next round on Iran or China.
items.tweetA: The ruble has a stablecoin, and the UK is sanctioning the exchanges that touch it. De-dollarization isn't happening via a BRICS currency, it's happening via a token on rails the West can only block at the on-ramp.
items.tweetB: Sanctions enforcement is moving from banks to exchanges. If you run a venue listing a sovereign-adjacent stablecoin, your compliance exposure just became your valuation risk.

items.title: Thailand opens BTC/ETH ETFs to mutual funds on Oct 16; Korean bank lends against BTC
items.idea: Thai SEC rules for locally listed BTC and ETH ETFs take effect Oct 16; funds must keep >=80% average net exposure and trade only on the SET. Separately, Jeonbuk Bank made what Edaily calls the first South Korean bank won loan secured by bitcoin, with the BTC held by a registered custodian and sold under court order on default. Also: Sui Foundation $30M into DATA Network (ex-Story), shutting its chain to rebuild on Sui; Zcash node team Zakura targets January for post-quantum signature opcodes.
items.angle: Quiet institutional plumbing: Asia is building regulated BTC access and BTC-collateral credit.
items.tweetA: Thailand lets mutual funds buy BTC/ETH ETFs from Friday. South Korea gets its first bank loan against bitcoin. Nobody tweets about these, and they're the boring plumbing that makes the next leg structurally different from 2021.
items.tweetB: A Korean bank lends won against BTC with court-ordered liquidation on default. Treat BTC as collateral in a legal system and the 'digital gold' debate is already over; the question is the haircut.

items.title: FedWatch: 19.4% odds of an October hike; BTC nearing 111/200DMA golden cross
items.idea: CME FedWatch has a 19.4% probability of an October Fed hike and 80.6% on hold. Adler notes BTC is above both the 111-day and 200-day SMAs and approaching a bullish 111/200 crossover. The weekly report covers long-term-holder selling pressure, expansion metrics, sell-pressure data and active addresses.
items.angle: A Fed that is hiking and BTC above its 200DMA is the opposite of the 2022 template. Rates are a swing factor only if CPI surprises Wednesday.
items.tweetA: Fed hike odds for October sit at 19%, BTC is above its 200DMA, and a 111/200 cross is a few days away. The market has decided the Fed is nearly done. CPI Wednesday is the only thing that argues.
items.tweetB: The Fed is raising rates and BTC is still above its 200-day. In 2022 that combination was impossible. Either the liquidity story changed, or the tightening isn't reaching the plumbing. See Capital Wars. $BTC

items.title: Is the Fed deliberately behind the curve? Markets are doing the tightening
items.idea: Howell argues Fed funds alone don't measure tightening: collateral conditions, bond volatility, the dollar and the yield curve are better indicators. Higher rates also raise Treasury interest payments to the private sector, partly offsetting the contraction, and the link between Fed funds and money-market liquidity is weak. The investment twist: if markets rather than the Fed are tightening, Bitcoin may behave less like a speculative asset and more like an ultra-long-duration asset.
items.angle: Reframes the Warsh Fed as a deliberate lag. Long-duration framing for BTC sets up the rate-sensitivity trade.
items.tweetA: A debt-saturated economy pays interest to the private sector, so each hike leaks stimulus. Fed funds is the least informative tightening gauge now. Watch collateral and bond vol instead. $TLT
items.tweetB: If the bond market is doing the tightening and Bitcoin is an ultra-long-duration asset, then BTC is a short-rates-volatility trade, not a risk-on trade. That changes which tape to watch.

charts.desc: One chart: Fed funds vs money-market liquidity, shown weakly linked. Worth opening.

items.title: 30% Q3 earnings growth: two-thirds tech, one-third from Micron and Nvidia alone
items.idea: LSEG expects ~30% y/y Q3 S&P earnings growth. About two-thirds comes from tech plus Meta, Alphabet and Amazon; about one third of the 30% comes from just Micron and Nvidia. Semis are expected up ~150%. Energy is expected up ~115% but is only ~3% of the S&P. The key AI data point is the updated capex plans of the five hyperscalers.
items.angle: S&P 'earnings growth' is two stocks. Single-name concentration risk sits inside the earnings line, not just the price index.
items.tweetA: A third of the S&P's 30% Q3 earnings growth is Micron and Nvidia. Two tickers. Earnings season is a referendum on the memory cycle with 498 supporting actors. $MU $NVDA
items.tweetB: Energy earnings +115% and it's 3% of the index. Semis +150% and it's the whole story. The headline growth number tells you nothing about the average company. Read the median, not the aggregate.

items.title: US crude oil rig count 462, highest since May 2025, still far below 600 in 2022
items.idea: US oil rigs rose 6 on the week to 462, the highest since May 2025 but well under the 600+ of 2022. Boockvar is long an oil-service stock and an offshore driller as beneficiaries.
items.angle: Supply response is slow with crude at $93. Shale discipline caps the upside for rigs vs price.
items.tweetA: Crude is $93 and the rig count is 462, still 25% below 2022. The shale response to a price spike is a fraction of what it used to be. That's why the oil curve stays steep. $OIH
items.tweetB: High prices, muted rig additions. The marginal barrel is now financed like a utility, not a startup. Oil service names get a longer, lower-beta cycle. $SLB

items.title: Contrarian: The Economist cover on bonds as a short-term top in yields
items.idea: Boockvar remains a long-term bear on long-duration bonds but thinks yields may have peaked temporarily because sentiment is too bearish, and notes that The Economist putting a theme on its cover usually marks the turn (h/t Rosenberg).
items.angle: Contrarian sentiment signal against the 'short bonds' consensus that MacroEdge also flags.
items.tweetA: Structural bear on duration, tactical bull. When The Economist puts bond vigilantes on the cover, the first move tends to be the wrong one. Positioning matters more than the thesis for the next 4 weeks. $TLT
items.tweetB: Everyone on X is telling you to short bonds because the labor market is great. That is the exact moment the trade stops paying. The thesis is right, the entry is crowded.

items.title: UMich sentiment 46.3, a five-month low and 13.6% below a year ago
items.idea: Preliminary October UMich sentiment fell 1.8 points to 46.3 vs 47.3 consensus, a five-month low, 13.6% below year-ago. Director Joanne Hsu: frustration over cost of living is mounting 'across the political spectrum' and consumers believe the economy has weakened since the start of the year.
items.angle: Sentiment at 46 into the midterms while All Star Charts says spending hit new highs. The gap is the story.
items.tweetA: Sentiment 46.3, near recession-era lows, and the S&P 500 is at 7,800. Consumers say the economy is worse and spend anyway. K-shaped isn't a slogan, it's why Visa makes new highs. $V
items.tweetB: Cost-of-living frustration 'across the political spectrum' with the midterms in three weeks. The question isn't what sentiment says about spending, it's what it says about incumbents.

items.title: Goldman: Mag7 is a record 22% of Prime book, while hedge funds sell semis
items.idea: S&P +1.2% to ~7,811. Hedge fund net exposure is near the bottom of its historical range even as gross is rebuilding. Funds aggressively sold Info Tech (semis, hardware) last week, yet Mag7 reached a record 22% of Prime US exposure. SPX downside protection is cheap (dispersion and low correlation) while VIX upside convexity is heavily bid. Goldman also flags crowded small-cap shorts, a long-bond squeeze setup, washed-out gold positioning and power as the most underappreciated AI bottleneck.
items.angle: Index calm, single-name violent. Selling semis while concentrating in Mag7 is the 'AI quality' trade.
items.tweetA: Hedge funds sold semis and hardware last week and pushed Mag7 to a record 22% of the book. They're not leaving AI, they're leaving the supply chain. Pay attention to who gets sold. $SOXX
items.tweetB: Cheap SPX puts, expensive VIX calls. The market is hedging a vol event, not an index drawdown. That's a bet on correlation spiking: the mirror image of Hi Mount's breadth message.

items.title: Goldman: washed-out gold positioning and a potential long-bond squeeze
items.idea: Within the same Goldman weekly: historically crowded small-cap shorts, a possible long-bond squeeze, washed-out gold positioning and improving equal-weight demand are the main non-index setups. Power remains the most underappreciated bottleneck in the AI buildout.
items.angle: Contrarian positioning screen: gold and long bonds both washed out while the dollar holds above 102.
items.tweetA: Gold positioning washed out, long bonds crowded short, small-cap shorts crowded. Goldman is describing three squeeze candidates in one note. $GLD $TLT $IWM
items.tweetB: Power is 'the most underappreciated bottleneck' per Goldman, and Oracle's Jupiter site just filed force majeure over how it would be powered. The thesis is already in the credit market.

items.title: Morgan Stanley: France 30y OAT over Bunds >150bp; deficit 5.4% vs 5.0% target
items.idea: Seth Carpenter sees real yields, nominal yields and private borrowing costs rising together. France's 30-year OAT spread to Bunds is above 150bp; MS expects the 2027 deficit at 5.4% of GDP vs the government's 5.0%, and stabilising debt requires a 5-percentage-point adjustment. The ECB is more likely to pause QT or reinvest than use the TPI. France is the 'warning shot' for a broader sovereign funding problem.
items.angle: ECB has little reason to backstop a fiscal repricing; EUR carry erodes. Pair with FX Daily's EUR note.
items.tweetA: 30-year OAT/Bund above 150bp, a 5.4% deficit and an election next year. MS says the ECB won't use the TPI, it'll just pause QT. That is a policy backstop priced as a hint. $FXE
items.tweetB: France needs a five-point fiscal adjustment before elections. The bond market just told you what probability it assigns to that. Where does the vigilante go after Paris?

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (FX Daily)
items.title: Dollar holds above 102 as Fed premium fades: 'cleanest dirty shirt'
items.idea: DXY stays above 102 even with the US 2-year off its late-Sept peak and October hike pricing pared, so it's a relative-value trade. EUR/USD ~1.12 under French fiscal stress, leveraged funds rebuilding EUR shorts; USD/CNY ~6.69 with firmer fixes as Beijing allows gradual appreciation amid European trade pushback (hybrid-vehicle caps reported). CPI Wednesday: core seen 0.2% m/m. Warsh speaks later this week.
items.angle: FX is trading relative dirt. Crowded EUR shorts plus CNY appreciation is a squeeze setup.
items.tweetA: DXY above 102 while the Fed premium leaves. The dollar isn't rising on US strength, it's rising on others' fiscal mess. The risk is EUR shorts at 1.12 getting stale and CNY quietly appreciating. $UUP $FXE
items.tweetB: China is letting USD/CNY drift to 6.69 while Europe imposes auto caps. Beijing is buying trade peace with a stronger currency. The 'weak yuan to export deflation' story is now a 2025 story.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman China)
items.title: Goldman: China is building 'the other AI market' and is structurally underowned
items.idea: Goldman's China team (Kinger Lau) argues China is assembling a self-contained AI stack. It has a capital disadvantage in frontier chips but dominates power equipment, batteries, transformers, rare-earth refining, PCB and optical modules. Two trades: exporters leveraged to Western capex, and domestic AI on self-sufficiency. China is ~13% of Goldman's global AI equity universe while global mutual funds put only ~5.8% of tech exposure in China.
items.angle: Physical-bottleneck suppliers (transformers, optics) are Chinese; the underweight is a positioning gap.
items.tweetA: China is 13% of the global AI equity universe and 5.8% of global fund tech allocations. Power equipment, optics, PCB, rare earths. The bottlenecks of Western AI are Chinese-made. The underweight isn't a view, it's an oversight. $KWEB
items.tweetB: Every US data center needs transformers and optical modules, and the supply chain runs through the country the US is trying to decouple from. 'Two AI systems' is the long-term bull case for both.

items.title: Korea's AI hangover: Kospi -22% in H2, turnover -70%, $131B foreign outflow
items.idea: After a ~100% H1 advance, Kospi is down 22% in H2. Turnover in the $4.3T market is -70% from the late-May peak and foreign investors have pulled $131B this year. Samsung and SK Hynix are more than half the index; Samsung fell despite a nearly ninefold jump in quarterly operating profit. Combined buybacks worth 55T won (~$41B) are nearly complete, and JPMorgan says they accounted for the bulk of $23B in market buy orders last month. Retail margin loans fell from 38.6T to ~33T won; brokerage cash from ~140T to ~100T. Taiex +70% YTD, 10% of members doubled vs 4.7% for Kospi.
items.angle: Memory earnings are fine, flows are not. The key is who bids once buybacks end. Taiwan is the preferred AI hardware vehicle.
items.tweetA: Samsung's operating profit rose almost ninefold and the stock fell. When great earnings can't lift a stock, the marginal buyer is gone. Korea's was the company itself ($41B in buybacks) and that program is ending. $EWY $SKM
items.tweetB: Taiex +70% with 10% of constituents doubled vs Korea's 4.7%. Same AI trade, different breadth. The market pays for breadth of the supply chain, not for the highest-margin chokepoint.

items.title: Kospi -3.65% to 6,384, worst day since Sept 2; Samsung -4.4% on OpenAI revenue shortfall report
items.idea: SK hynix fell 4.5% in Seoul Monday as the Kospi dropped 3.65% to 6,384, its biggest one-day decline since September 2. Samsung fell 4.4%, with analysts citing renewed AI-bubble worries after reports OpenAI's revenue was lower than previously reported. US futures: SPX +0.06%, Nasdaq -0.16%, crude $93.13 (+1.59%). US bond market is closed for Columbus Day.
items.angle: Continuation of the Korea unwind, catalyst is an OpenAI revenue miss. Watch US memory names at the open.
items.tweetA: Kospi -3.65% on an OpenAI revenue miss report. The single biggest customer's revenue is the memory cycle's soft spot. US futures are flat, so the question is whether $MU opens as the next shoe.
items.tweetB: OpenAI revenue below reported, and a Korea tape that was already cracked. The AI trade's weak link isn't demand for chips, it's the revenue that pays for them. See Borrowed Time. $MU $NVDA

items.title: Hunterbrook discloses Meta short: Muse downloads -8.1% w/w, net adds -62%
items.idea: Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in Meta after an affiliated Hunterbrook Media report using TickerTrends data: downloads of Meta's Muse fell 8.1% week over week to ~165,000/day, and net daily user additions slowed ~62% to ~74,000 in the first week of October.
items.angle: App-data short thesis on a first-party AI product. Meta is also the biggest off-balance-sheet SPV user (Hyperion).
items.tweetA: Hunterbrook is short Meta on Muse download data: 165k/day and net adds -62%. A consumer AI product decelerating while capex leaves the balance sheet via SPVs is the exact mismatch bears want. $META
items.tweetB: Meta funds Hyperion off-balance-sheet at $27B while its AI app slows. If the product disappoints, the footnote becomes the story.

items.title: IREN +5% premarket on report of multiyear Anthropic AI-cloud deal
items.idea: IREN rose ~5% premarket after The Information reported it signed a multiyear AI cloud services deal with Anthropic. Neither party has confirmed; terms undisclosed. Also: BofA lifted its Alibaba HK price target to HK$175 from HK$172, saying the expected earnings inflection is not priced in; BABA rose as much as 3% in Hong Kong with Citi and Jefferies also raising targets.
items.angle: Ex-bitcoin-miner neoclouds are now the capacity layer for labs, and the credit layer for them is the weak link.
items.tweetA: Anthropic reportedly signs a multiyear compute deal with IREN, a former bitcoin miner. The AI labs are renting capacity from whoever has power, and miners have power. $IREN
items.tweetB: Same day OpenAI revenue disappoints, Anthropic reportedly adds compute. Funding gaps between labs are widening, and the neoclouds are the ones holding the contracts. $CRWV

items.title: Brazil runoff poll: Flávio Bolsonaro 52.7% vs Lula 47.3% (valid votes)
items.idea: Ipespe/Abrapel poll released Saturday shows Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of President Lula 52.7% to 47.3% of valid votes in the 25 October runoff (49% to 44% raw). Brazil's exchange is closed Monday for a holiday.
items.angle: Binary event for BRL, Ibovespa and Brazilian rates two weeks out.
items.tweetA: Brazil's runoff poll flips: Flávio Bolsonaro 52.7, Lula 47.3 on valid votes. The market is closed today, so the first reaction is Tuesday. Fiscal credibility is the trade. $EWZ
items.tweetB: Three weeks to the US midterms, thirteen days to Brazil's runoff. Two big electorates tell pollsters the economy has weakened. Cost of living is a global incumbent tax.

items.title: 'Peak apathy': nobody believes in a downside case for a federalized market
items.idea: MacroEdge sees cycle-high apathy across tech and everything else. Semis will be 're-discovered' as commodity-like; Kospi called a 'dumpster fire'. The AI ecosystem has broad political backstops (esp. data center construction), but the author expects an unwind this quarter or next as construction signals flash, environmental opposition rises and financing gets harder as demand wobbles. No profit moat for nearly any business in the space. Oil and bonds will drive the rest of the year; emergency reserves are draining with 'zero plan'. Week ahead: CPI Wed, PPI Thu; bond market closed today.
items.angle: Bearish AI-capex thesis from the energy-first desk, consistent with Borrowed Time and Korea.
items.tweetA: No profit moat for nearly any AI business, a federal backstop for the buildout, and construction signals about to flash. 'Peak apathy' is when the downside case costs least to hedge. $SMH
items.tweetB: Emergency oil reserves draining with no plan. Everyone is arguing about the Fed, but the biggest swing factor for inflation is a barrel that costs $93 and a reserve that can't refill.

items.title: AI debt: $466B raised through September vs $216B in all of 2025
items.idea: Morgan Stanley counts $466B of AI-related debt through September, more than double the $216B in all of 2025. The largest AI spenders' share of IG non-financial issuance went from ~2% to 19%. MS expects the biggest spenders to reinvest >40% of revenue in 2027, above the ~32% peak of dot-com fibre builders. Alphabet and Amazon had negative FCF in Q2; Alphabet went from >$60B/yr of buybacks to zero and issued $50B of new shares. SpaceX is seeking $40B to buy Nvidia chips. The 5-year Treasury is above 5% after September's Fed hike.
items.angle: Hyperscalers are now net borrowers; AI issuance competing with Treasuries is itself a driver of yields.
items.tweetA: Tech capex at 40% of revenue in 2027 vs 32% at the dot-com fibre peak. Alphabet went from $60B in buybacks to issuing $50B in stock. This is no longer a cash-flow story. $GOOGL $AMZN
items.tweetB: AI issuers went from 2% to 19% of IG supply in one year. Hyperscaler bonds compete with Treasuries for the same buyers, so the AI buildout is part of why the 5-year is above 5%. The boom raises its own cost of capital.

items.title: Oracle at BBB-, CDS up ~4x; Project Jupiter lessee files force majeure
items.idea: Oracle is rated BBB- by S&P, one notch above junk, and its CDS has roughly quadrupled in a year. Project Jupiter (~1GW in New Mexico for Oracle/OpenAI Stargate) got $18B of bank loans last November; after permit delays on power, Oracle sent a force majeure notice in late September, delaying lease start. $300B of Oracle's $455B backlog is tied to OpenAI. On a $10B 10-year loan each extra point costs $100M a year.
items.angle: Weak link of the AI credit chain: lender, developer and tenant all hinge on one counterparty and a power permit.
items.tweetA: Oracle: BBB-, CDS 4x in a year, $300B of a $455B backlog tied to one customer, and a flagship site invoking force majeure over power. Today's OpenAI revenue miss rhymes with all four. $ORCL
items.tweetB: The Jupiter loan was priced before the Fed's hike and before the 5-year crossed 5%. Every lease slip makes the bank's collateral less money and the buyer of that loan more demanding.

items.title: $1.1T of unstarted data-center leases and $3.4T of total commitments sit off balance sheet
items.idea: Morgan Stanley counts ~$1.1T of signed-but-not-started data center leases at the five largest spenders, off balance sheet until tenants move in; adding chip purchase commitments and guarantees it passes $3.4T. Meta's Hyperion: Meta owns 20%, Blue Owl funds 80% via SPV Beignet Investor LLC, which raised ~$27.3B of bonds due 2049. Meta records no liability for its residual guarantee; EY flagged it as a critical audit matter. S&P will count Alphabet's ~$17B of guaranteed leases as debt once they begin. Depreciation at MSFT, ORCL, META, GOOGL could exceed $520B over three years.
items.angle: The financial-statement lag: construction in progress isn't depreciated, so 2026 EPS flatters 2028.
items.tweetA: $3.4T of AI commitments, most of it off balance sheet. Meta's Hyperion alone is $27B of bonds that Meta doesn't record. The auditor called it a critical matter. The footnote is the balance sheet now. $META
items.tweetB: Data centers under construction don't depreciate, so today's EPS is flattered by the same build that will crush it in 2027-28. $520B of depreciation is coming for four income statements.

items.title: 'Steam is coming out of the AI trade', and it can't unwind without collateral damage
items.idea: BUSHY beta portfolio: 8.43% annualized vol, Sharpe 1.51, Sortino 3.09, with little direct exposure to the central AI trade beyond index length in the CTA sleeve. September drawdown mostly recovered; author sees steam leaving AI and doubts it can unwind without damage in other risk assets, so is not taking excessive risks for Q4.
items.angle: A systematic macro PM sizing down because AI unwinding would be correlated across everything.
items.tweetA: A macro PM with Sharpe 1.51 and almost no AI exposure still says AI can't unwind without collateral damage. If you're underweight the trade, you still own it through the index and your credit.
items.tweetB: The AI trade is 22% of hedge-fund books at Goldman's Prime and the biggest share of index earnings growth. 'We don't own it' doesn't mean 'we're not exposed'.

items.title: 26th time in 55 years: S&P record high with more new lows than new highs
items.idea: S&P closed at a record last Tuesday while NYSE+Nasdaq has had more new lows than new highs for 30 consecutive days and the trend in new lows vs highs for 20 days. It is the 26th time in 55+ years the S&P made a new high on this breadth, and all prior instances were followed in short order by index weakness. Only 1 in 10 global markets are above their 50-day average, <4 in 10 above their 200-day. Mid-caps broke down vs large-caps, small-caps close behind, and the earnings revision trend is breaking down.
items.angle: Breadth divergence plus Goldman's concentration data and Boockvar's earnings concentration. Three independent confirmations.
items.tweetA: 26th time in 55 years: S&P record high, more new lows than new highs. All 25 previous times ended in index weakness 'in relatively short order'. 30 consecutive days of negative breadth. $SPY
items.tweetB: Three notes this morning, three ways to say the same thing: 22% Mag7 in hedge fund books, two stocks make a third of earnings growth, and breadth on 30 straight negative days. The index is a single trade.

items.title: 'Pushing on a String': more hikes won't fix tariff and energy-driven inflation
items.idea: Ironsides argues further rate hikes are poorly matched to energy- and tariff-driven price pressure and will worsen federal interest costs, housing and CRE; any disinflation from hikes is likely swamped by the inflationary effect of financing government debt. Earnings growth is concentrated in tech and AI infrastructure; they stay in cash as the most attractive hedge until breadth improves.
items.angle: Fiscal dominance argument against a hiking Fed, which is the other side of Capital Wars.
items.tweetA: Hikes can't lower the price of oil or tariffs. They can raise the interest bill. If the 5-year is above 5%, the Fed is raising the deficit it's trying to tame. Fiscal dominance in plain sight.
items.tweetB: Ironsides is in cash, Hi Mount sees a bear market under the surface, Blind Squirrel is de-risking. The macro desks are pointing the same way. The question is who is positioned the other way.

items.title: Trump's Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire': Zelensky wasn't told; Russia hit Kharkiv within hours
items.idea: The White House announced Sunday an immediate ceasefire on attacks on Russian and Ukrainian energy infrastructure; Zelensky said he had not been informed. Within hours Russia bombed Ukrainian energy installations including a power plant in Kharkiv. Frankopan calls it 'diplomatic fiction' and a gift to Putin for nothing.
items.angle: Energy-ceasefire headlines are moving oil sentiment, but the FX market ignored it (see FX Daily).
items.tweetA: A ceasefire that one of the two belligerents didn't know about, followed by strikes on a power plant in Kharkiv. The market that trades headlines should price this as zero information. Oil traders are looking at the barrel, not the communiqué. $CL_F
items.tweetB: Energy infrastructure is the one target class where a ceasefire could be verified. That it failed in hours says a lot about who has leverage. Europe's winter gas curve depends on it. $TTF

items.title: GLP-1s: 11% of US adults, $76B of sales vs $63B for generative AI
items.idea: US adults taking a GLP-1 for weight loss went from 3% (2024) to 11%. By end-2025 GLP-1 sales ($76B) exceeded generative AI revenue ($63B), and more than twice as many Americans pay for GLP-1s as for AI. US obesity peaked near 40% in 2022 and is down three points as of July 2026; new diabetes diagnoses have flatlined; GLP-1s were 14% of US drug spend in 2025. Retatrutide (May) shows a ~10-point efficacy improvement vs 2021 semaglutide.
items.angle: A technology bigger than AI by revenue today, with population-level data effects.
items.tweetA: $76B of GLP-1 sales vs $63B of generative AI revenue, and 11% of US adults are on one. The obesity rate is down three points in four years. AI is the story and GLP-1s are the larger economy. $LLY $NVO
items.tweetB: More Americans pay for GLP-1s than for AI. If a pharmaceutical is the largest consumer technology of the decade, what does a market priced on AI adoption curves miss?

items.title: GLP-1 price collapse: $1,349 list to $13/month in India; Lilly cut price 13%, volume +60%
items.idea: Semaglutide listed at $1,349/month in 2021; Novo's cash price fell to $499 then $199 from February. After India's patent expired on March 20, a month costs ~$13: 99% below original US list. Lilly's Q2 realized price fell 13% and volume rose 60%. Indian sales growth fell to 2% in June after 58% in April. Persistence is the risk: 32% on drug at one year and 15% at two (UK), half quit within a year (Denmark). US patents run to 2032 (semaglutide) and 2036 (tirzepatide), and four Medicaid programs dropped obesity coverage.
items.angle: Volume-for-price is working at Lilly, but adherence is the real churn variable. Indian generics are a price anchor for 2032.
items.tweetA: Lilly cut realized price 13% and got 60% more volume. India's generic is $13 a month. Persistence is 15% at two years in the UK. The business is a retention game, not a launch game. $LLY
items.tweetB: A $13/month generic in India and a $1,349 list price in 2021. The 99% price gap is a global arbitrage that US patents hold until 2032. Medicaid dropping coverage shows who bears the gap.

items.title: GLP-1 shopping baskets: chocolate -18pp, gum +24pp, mouthwash +20pp
items.idea: UK GLP-1 users spend less and shift from chocolate (down 18 percentage points) to gum (+24) and mouthwash (+20). Hershey is promoting gum and mints against 'Ozempic breath' and nutrition bar sales rose 12% in Q2. Semaglutide plus therapy cut heavy drinking days 41% vs 26% with therapy alone, and GLP-1 use is linked to 50% fewer substance-abuse deaths. Modelling suggests people without a high school diploma gain most (14% more lifetime social value). One study found no insurer medical-cost savings over five years ($0.22 more spending per $1).
items.angle: Consumer staples second-order effects: the substitution is visible in baskets before it is in earnings.
items.tweetA: GLP-1 users in the UK buy 18 points less chocolate and 24 points more gum. The consumer-staples impact is already visible in baskets and Hershey is pivoting. Which food category is most exposed to a 11% adult penetration? $HSY
items.tweetB: Semaglutide cuts heavy drinking days 41% vs 26%, and substance-abuse deaths 50% lower. A 'temperance technology' is a bear case for alcohol that no beverage analyst has modelled.

items.title: TasteVal: AI research taste doubling every 3.0 months; Opus 5.5 beats expert baseline at 1/30 the cost
items.idea: P-Zero's TasteVal tests experimental research taste across 8 frontier-AI-development tasks against 24 expert baseliners (OpenAI, DeepMind, NVIDIA, MSR). Frontier models' experimental research taste has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0). The best model, Opus 5.5, exceeds the human baseline with a 2.30x compute multiplier at ~1/30 of the cost per attempt. Clark moves his estimate for full recursive self-improvement from 2028 to 2027.
items.angle: Direct measure of the RSI input variable (creativity/taste). A 3-month doubling is faster than compute scaling.
items.tweetA: Research taste doubling every 3 months, best model above the human expert baseline at 1/30 the cost per attempt. Jack Clark pulls RSI forward a year to 2027. If that's even half right, nothing else in this week's tape matters. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The AI debt market is pricing a 2028 revenue ramp. The researcher closest to the frontier is pulling the capability timeline forward. The mismatch between financing assumptions and capability progress cuts both ways.

items.title: US open-weight returns, but Reflection's Beam (501B) and Mistral Large 4 both trail Chinese models
items.idea: Reflection's Beam: 501B MoE (23B active), pretrained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then RL on ~10.5K GPUs for four weeks; 23.8T tokens; 1M RL environments; 3-4x less inference compute than GLM-5.2 at comparable reasoning. It scores below GLM-5.3 (DeepSWE 44.4 vs 61; MCP Atlas 78.7 vs 84.2). Mistral Large 4 (3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs) scores 62 on DeepSWE vs 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3, but Terminal-Bench 28.3 vs 41.9. Both plan open-weight releases this month. Separately, on Humanity's Sixth Sense (visual reasoning), GPT 6 Astra scores 53.6 vs 93.1 for humans; GLM-5.3-flash 26.8, Kimi K3 25.5.
items.angle: Chinese open-weight leads on coding/agentic; Western open models compete on token efficiency and cyber.
items.tweetA: Reflection's Beam used 6,144 GB300s for four weeks and still trails GLM-5.3 on coding agents. The US open-weight comeback is compute-rich and capability-poor. China's lead comes from the RL environment grind, not hardware. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Mistral Large 4 is the strongest Western open-weight model and still behind Kimi K3 on DeepSWE (62 vs 68). Europe's AI sovereignty product is one generation behind a Chinese startup. Does 'sovereign' mean 'second-best by choice'?

items.title: 'The AI race extends beyond Earth': space as a compounding advantage for AI
items.idea: AI Frontiers argues AI will speed the build-out of space-based power, compute and manufacturing in the 2030s on Starship lift. Spacecraft redesigned for AI rather than crew survive debris that would kill a crewed vessel. First movers get an industrial flywheel, domain awareness (denying others access) and self-replicating probes. Clark expects solar-system activity to be dominated by autonomous machines.
items.angle: Space-based compute/power as a power-bottleneck workaround; strategic denial dimension.
items.tweetA: AI redesigns spacecraft around no humans, so a debris hit that kills the ISS only scratches an uncrewed vessel. Space economics improves when you drop life support. Power is the AI bottleneck and orbit has unlimited sun. $RKLB
items.tweetB: SpaceX is raising $40B to buy Nvidia chips. The link between compute, power and orbit is already in someone's term sheet. First mover in space isn't a flag, it's a flywheel.

items.title: DOE labs knit supercomputers together for federated AI training, but ~100x off frontier scale
items.idea: NNSA's Sandia, LLNL and LANL trained a LLaMA-based model across El Capitan (AMD MI300A) and NVIDIA H100 machines while keeping restricted data on site (1B/8B/70B scale). A separate project fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on chemistry data across ~1,700 GPUs on Aurora, Polaris, Frontier and Perlmutter. Clark notes governments would need to lash together ~100k chips to be near parity with industry.
items.angle: Sovereign compute pooling is possible; scale gap is the constraint. Federated training across vendors (AMD, NVIDIA, Intel) works.
items.tweetA: Four DOE supercomputers and three vendors' GPUs trained one model without moving the restricted data. The technical barrier to sovereign AI isn't architecture, it's scale: ~100x short of frontier. Whoever closes that gap writes the policy.
items.tweetB: Federated training across AMD, NVIDIA and Intel hardware is the quiet counterpoint to the CUDA moat story. If the framework runs on mixed clusters, hardware lock-in weakens. $AMD

items.title: Venture math: 65 of 100 deals lose money, 6% of deals make 60% of returns
items.idea: Correlation Ventures (21,640 US deals, 2004-2013): 65% returned less than invested, 25% returned 1-5x, 6% 5-10x, 4% 10x+. Horsley Bridge/a16z: ~6% of investments produced ~60% of returns, and top funds lost money on more deals. Kauffman: 69 of 88 funds failed to beat the market after risk and illiquidity. A $100m fund with 10% ownership must sell companies totalling $3.4B to hit a 3x net; a $1B fund needs $34B. Carta Q1 2026: <20% of 2017-18 vintage funds have returned even the capital invested.
items.angle: Why VCs say 'too small for us' and why DPI is now the headline metric: vintage 2017-18 funds aren't distributing.
items.tweetA: Fewer than 20% of 2017-18 vintage VC funds have returned a dollar of invested capital. Nine years in. The J-curve is a straight line down for most LPs; the paper marks are doing the work.
items.tweetB: A $1B fund needs $34B in exits to deliver 3x. That's a different business than a $100M fund. The AI mega-round era forces VC into the same power-law math as public-market concentration.

items.title: Visa breaks out to all-time highs, ~$700B market cap, 8.36% of S&P Financials
items.idea: Visa has broken to new all-time highs after more than a year of consolidation, with higher highs and higher lows intact. It is the third-largest weight in S&P Financials (8.36%) and worth ~$700B; the author argues it has a real shot at $1T. Short-dated calls bought in the author's trading room tripled in a day. (Promotional framing for a paid room.)
items.angle: Spending bellwether breaking out against UMich at 46 is the divergence to explain.
items.tweetA: Visa at all-time highs while consumer sentiment is at a five-month low. Payments volume is nominal and inflation inflates it. The stock is a toll on the price level, not a read on happiness. $V
items.tweetB: Sentiment 46.3, Visa at ATH. K-shaped consumption means top-income spending drives the card volumes. The index reads the top 10%'s wallet, not the median household. $MA
